Its extended handle lets you glide it smoothly across the face, neck, and body, and practitioners and users regularly report support for relaxation, circulation, and nervous system regulation. rec7Vm5QNrDbc9sdb.Bio: Chance Garton is the host and producer of the Innerverse Podcast, where for over a decade he has investigated consciousness, mythology, symbolism, terrain health, and the psychosomatic language of the human body and mind. A biofield tuning practitioner, he uses tuning forks to help clients resolve physical symptoms, break negative patterns, and return to energetic coherence.
rec7Vm5QNrDbc9sdb.Name: Chance Garton
rec7Vm5QNrDbc9sdb.Role: Host of the Innerverse Podcast, biofield tuning practitioner & researcher

recbqsYSV8FGvCA28.Bio: Kyle Denton is a community herbalist and medicine maker from Wisconsin who founded Tippecanoe Herbs with his wife Serena Marinelli in 2015. From their Milwaukee apothecary they craft small batch remedies from locally harvested and organic herbs, working from a bio terrain philosophy that blends Ayurveda with Western herbalism. He also runs Root Radical Herbal Academy, has taught for over a decade through his annual three season class and his Milwaukee herb walks, and sees clients as the Tuning Herbalist, using tuning forks to read the biofield. His Substack and podcast, Resonature, explore the interval between vital herbalism, biofield tuning and cosmology.
recbqsYSV8FGvCA28.Name: Kyle Denton
recbqsYSV8FGvCA28.Role: Community herbalist, founder of Tippecanoe Herbs

fields.Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "Spirit Precedes Form: The Vitalist Premise", "body": "Chance opens by arguing that the physicalist view, that an object's qualities emerge from its material composition, is the most distorting precept of the Kali Yuga, and he points to the hard problem of consciousness, near death experiences, out of body travel and synchronicity as evidence that spirit precedes form. Melissa Kupsch, director of RMDY Academy and CEO of RMDY Collective, says homeopathy demonstrates that same principle, and Kyle Denton of Tippecanoe Herbs joins as co-host because he is a clinical herbalist who already works with homeopathy. Melissa contends the medicine was widely used historically, then suppressed, and is now in a genuine resurgence."}, {"title": "Taking the Whole Case, Not the Seven Minute Version", "body": "Melissa describes how a homeopath takes a case: at least ninety minutes, compared with the roughly seven minutes she says an Australian bulk billed Medicare consultation allows from walking in to walking out with a prescription. She asks clients for a timeline from birth, even from the womb if the mother carried trauma, right up to the present, and says many people have never been asked that question. She calls the search for the origin point the never well since, and explains that a chronic pattern recurring in cycles signals, in her framework, something blocking the vital force rather than a discrete disease to be named."}, {"title": "Resonance, Adaptation and the Story Underneath", "body": "Kyle describes customers at his herb shop drawn to a wall of jars, pulling one down like a tarot card and asking what it is good for, then recognising themselves in his answer, which he calls a cousin of homeopathic proving and a harmonizing of inner narrative rather than a fix for a disease. Chance connects this to biofield tuning, where memories surface at specific points in the energy field, and argues that trauma work is about tracing how a personality adapted. Melissa agrees, saying habits people carry guilt about, from gym compulsion to an ADHD label, are adaptations rather than identity."}, {"title": "Sympathy Versus Suppression, and the Search for the Simillimum", "body": "Melissa distinguishes acting in sympathy with the body, as with saunas or fasting, from antipathic approaches she says can amount to green pharmacy. She contrasts classical homeopathy, which hunts the simillimum across the totality of a case, with the Narayani line, bottles labelled by disease name that combine several remedies, and with the fertility protocols she used in her first five years of practice. Kyle asks whether homeopathy has an equivalent of the doctrine of signatures, and Melissa points to the Prisma materia medica, the oyster shell behind Calcarea carbonica, and the match head image behind Phosphorus."}, {"title": "Who Makes the Medicine, and the Resurgence", "body": "Melissa says her former lecturer Peter, who first introduced her to homeopathy and now co teaches the academy, works on spagyric bases for remedies and has sourced material from Sajah Popham. Kyle describes living minutes from an anthroposophical medicine clinic near some of the first Rudolf Steiner farms, where makers emphasise an upward vortex when succussing, unlike Hahnemann banging the vial on his Bible. Both stress the maker's intention and state of mind. Melissa reports 570 sign ups to the academy's first cohort, against a usual 30 students a year, and a homeopathic hospital being built in Australia."}]
fields.Intro Paragraph 1: Australian homeopath Melissa Kupsch of the RMDY Collective joins InnerVerse to explore the art and science of vitalistic healing. From her own miraculous cure that opened the path, to the way remedies connect mind, body, and spirit, Melissa shares why homeopathy is more relevant than ever.
fields.Intro Paragraph 2: We cover case stories, symptom patterns, spagyric innovations, and the deeper philosophy behind homeopathy, not just “what works,” but why it works. This episode is a journey into resonance, vitality, and mind/body medicine.

fields.Plus Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "The Miasm Map of Disease", "body": "Melissa lays out homeopathy's five dominant miasms: psora from scabies, gonorrhea's psychotic pattern, tuberculosis, syphilis, and carcinosin. She traces how a grandparent's suppressed tuberculosis can surface as asthma or eczema two generations later, and how the syphilitic miasm shows up as compulsive hand washing, left handedness, twin births, and a thin veil to the spirit world in musicians and psychics. Nosodes, made from the diseased tissue itself, feed that inherited energy back to the body so it can finally resolve, rather than simply suppressing another generation's symptoms."}, {"title": "Terrain Over Germ Theory", "body": "Kyle and Melissa dismantle contagion as the real driver of illness, pointing out that no isolated contagious agent has ever been proven and that mucus transfer experiments never reproduce symptoms. They argue belief in germs itself primes people to mirror a sick person's symptoms through field resonance, not infection. Melissa traces homeopathic prophylaxis back to Hahnemann protecting a girl from scarlet fever with Belladonna, and to Cuba's 2007 mass dosing against leptospirosis, arguing homeopathic hospitals once saw under 1 percent mortality against over 30 percent in conventional wards."}, {"title": "Energy That Skips a Generation", "body": "Chance describes a biofield tuning client whose unexplained heart palpitations traced back to a great grandmother terrified in the London Blitz while her husband was away fighting, and how clearing that ancestor's fear eased the client's symptoms. Melissa matches this with cases where a grandmother's needed remedy cured a grandchild instead: one girl's compulsive rash and mouth stuffing resolved with a remedy over six months, and a boy's throat clearing tic vanished once he took the remedy his grandmother, born on his same birthday, actually needed."}, {"title": "Fibonacci and the Right Dose", "body": "Kyle and Melissa compare notes on blending remedy potencies rather than picking just one. Melissa's RMDY Academy combines multiple potencies, from 30C up to 1M, into a single home accord bottle so a patient's own vital force selects the strength it needs, avoiding the harsh aggravations that come from too big a gap between dose and need. Kyle builds his herbal formulas the same way, layering doses in Fibonacci proportions because he sees that spiral, from sunflowers to pinecones to the body's own organs, as nature's harmonizing pattern."}, {"title": "Grief Remedies and a Growing Movement", "body": "Asked for something to help him access buried sadness, Melissa recommends Ignatia or Aurum Metallicum, the gold remedy for dutiful, talented people who suppress grief until it floods out. She closes by describing RMDY Academy's first cohort of 570 students, evidence of what she calls the great resurgence of homeopathy, and her goal of rebuilding homeopathic hospitals, starting with one already under construction in Australia, so more people can access this medicine of the spirit."}]
